en: The *Prakaraṇapañcikā*, composed by the Great Professor Śālikanātha Miśra, who bore the yoke of the tradition of the illustrious Guru Prabhākara.
Adorned with the commentary titled *Nyāyasiddhi* and the critical notes (*ṭippaṇī*) on difficult passages,
this work is named *Vimalāñjana*.
The Seventh Chapter:
The Declaration of the Chapter’s Subject Matter.
When the relationship between both word and meaning is established as being non-human (apauruṣeya), [the Veda is authoritative]. 678.
The validity of Vedic statements is what is established therein. // 1 //
Thus:
if the relationship between words and their meanings were indeed of human origin,

then, because humans have the capacity to establish conventions only regarding objects that fall within the scope of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [the Veda would be subject to human error].

Furthermore, since the subject matter of the Veda consists of a unique causal efficacy (*apūrvakārya*), there is no scope for other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) therein; consequently, no linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) can exist for it.

And since it is accepted that what lacks a convention cannot be expressive, the authority of Vedic sentences would become impossible to attain. Thus, this effort to establish the relationship between non-human words and their meanings is indeed purposeful.
The prima facie position is according to the Vaiśeṣika school:
therein, the proponents of the Vedas, asserting that the world was created by the Lord (Īśvara), declare that the relationship between word and meaning is of human origin. (2)
Thus:

for when there exists a beginningless succession of usage by elders, the relationship of signifier and signified between word and meaning—established through the usage of elders—is proven to be non-human (apauruṣeya).
To explain: children, hearing the speech of elders engaged in activity for their own purposes, [perceive] immediately following the hearing of the words...

Observing that a specific cognition regarding a particular object arises through a specific movement, they determine that the word possesses denotative power; yet even those elders, when they were children, were themselves trained in this very same manner.
And from those elders whom they acquired proficiency, they too acquired proficiency in this very same manner, and they [in turn] from other elders.
Even without a person who establishes the convention, the relationship between word and meaning is indeed established through beginningless usage among elders;
this implies that the usage of elders is itself beginningless.
Indeed, it is not at all tenable that the succession of the linguistic usage of the elders (*vṛddha*) is beginningless.
For instance—let your honors understand this: everything, such as the body, the world, and so forth, is determined to possess constituent parts (*sāvayava*).
And whatever indeed possesses constituent parts, [is subject to origination].
We perceive a cloth that has acquired its own existence through the interlacing of threads, and a mat whose being is produced by the conjunction of reeds; both of these possess parts.
This same principle applies to all composite wholes, descending from the ultimate wholes down to the dyads.
Furthermore, the mutual conjunction of atoms must necessarily be admitted as being produced by the action of one or produced by the action of both;
and such action in atoms is asserted to arise from the conjunction of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*).
As it has been said: “The first motion of the atom and of the mind is caused by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa),” Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 5.2.13.
Since no other cause exists, and the unseen force is not capable of producing an effect unless it has attained its own functional operation (svavṛtti).
Because it is insentient, like an axe;
for an insentient object is not observed to function unless presided over by a sentient being.
Indeed, an axe does not proceed toward the act of cutting without being presided over by a carpenter.

Thus, it must necessarily be accepted on the strength of observation that the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), which is not inherent in the field (*kṣetra*) and is presided over by a conscious being, is sufficient for the production of effects.
Nor should it be deliberated here that those very individuals who are the knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*) might themselves be the presiding agents of those unseen forces.
Because they are ignorant;

for they are not able to know, either by their own nature or through their effects, the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) which, though inherent in them, possess the characteristics of dharma and adharma.
And whoever is able to know something according to its essential nature or through its effects,
he alone is its presiding controller.
Just as a carpenter [requires] an axe,

so too there must be accepted a certain superior conscious being who is distinct from the individual knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*), who possesses an inconceivable power and majesty consisting in the direct perception of the merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) inherent in all knowers of the field, who is eternally established, and who is independent.
Nor should it be asked by what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that power of directly perceiving dharma and adharma— which is impossible for ordinary field-knower-souls (*kṣetrajña*)—
is understood; for by the very same means of valid cognition through which His existence is understood, His power of knowledge is likewise understood.
This very [entity], possessing an inherent power of cognition, is the object of inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭānumāna*).
For this very reason, there is no room for the objection, "How will it exercise its control?
Nor is there any room for the further objection, "What is the purpose of its exercising such control?"
That [position] has been refuted by the acceptance of the inference based on the excellence of consciousness (*cetanā*).
For the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) is conscious and acts with a view toward his own purpose;
however, that [proposed creator], being distinct from the *kṣetrajña*, acts independently and without regard for any purpose at all.
Therefore, due to this very sovereignty, its occasional activity is logically consistent; moreover, that sovereignty is to be understood solely through the inference from existence (*sattānumāna*),
and does not depend upon any separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, it is established that the body, the world, and so forth—which originate from that [Brahman]—possess a beginning and are produced;
likewise, by virtue of having a beginning, they are perishable.
For all conditioned entities (bhāvas) are subject to destruction as an inevitable certainty.
Likewise, since jars and other such objects have been previously perceived,
there is no beginninglessness to the tradition of usage among the elders.
Therefore, one must accept that the capacity of a word to cause the comprehension of its meaning arises solely from the convention established by persons.
The doubt that denotative power is based on convention:
Furthermore, it is beyond dispute that in words such as "Devadatta," denotative power is based on human convention;
seeing this, it is appropriate to infer that the same is the case for words such as "cow" as well.

For this indeed is the scope of the inference based on general observation (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa): that which is observed in one place is inferred elsewhere. This indeed is the scope of the inference based on general observation: that which is observed in one place...
It is inferred elsewhere;
moreover, the claim that words such as "Devadatta" possess an inherent capacity to convey their own meanings is also not correct,
because there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*).
Furthermore, convention has no function regarding restriction, because it would follow that a cognition of an unrestricted object would arise prior to the convention.
This is said merely to point out a difficulty: even in the case of words such as "cow," the comprehension of a restricted meaning depends entirely upon human convention.

Intrinsic power to convey its own meaning is indeed efficacious for the comprehension of specific objects; therefore, enough of this excessive insistence on a doctrine that undermines the very meaning already established.

Furthermore, since the Blessed One—who is proven by the force of the aforementioned means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), who is uniquely skilled in the creation of the entire world, and who is the direct perceiver of dharma and adharma—is established as their author, this rejection of the position that the Vedas are of human origin by the Mīmāṃsakas is based solely on their prejudice.
And as for the numerous *mantras* and *arthavādas* that declare this very meaning directly, their description [in other ways] is not the final position (*siddhānta*).
For it is accepted that the relationship between a word and its meaning is innate (*autpattika*). 707–708. The relationship of a word with its meaning is considered to be eternal.
For the usage of elders has a beginningless continuity.
Thus.

The venerable Jaimini, the foremost among those who know the meaning of the Vedas and a treasury of all methods of reasoning, maintains that the relationship between the non-human (apauruṣeya) word and its meaning is eternal.
For he considered that, although the denotative power of words such as "Devadatta" is based on human convention,
it is nevertheless impossible to apply such an inference to words like "cow."
Because the effect characterized by the comprehension of meaning can be accounted for otherwise, it is inconclusive;
for even from the knowledge of a word's expressive power regarding its own referent—which is based on the linguistic usage of elders—children are observed to comprehend the meaning of words.
Therefore, it is not possible to conclude with certainty that [the relationship between word and meaning] is nothing but convention (*saṅketa*).
Moreover, it is a matter of direct perception that the comprehension of meaning from words such as "cow" is based solely on the knowledge of their expressive power (*śakti*).
And when a cause is directly perceived, it is not possible to infer another cause.
However, in the case of proper names such as "Devadatta," for whom the comprehension of meaning is based upon convention (*saṅketa*), [the situation is different].
For him, the convention alone is the cause.
Furthermore, for those who understand the denotative capacity of words merely through observing linguistic usage and thereby comprehend the meaning,
it is precisely the knowledge of the power [of the word] produced by the observation of usage that is the cause of their comprehension of the meaning.
It is not a convention; rather,
in that case, both linguistic usage and the comprehension of meaning are preceded by convention.
Likewise, even the cognition of denotative capacity (*vācakatva*) is preceded by that [usage].

However, in the case of words such as "cow" (*go*), since linguistic usage is possible for everyone through the mere cognition of the expressive power (*śakti*), the comprehension of meaning occurs; thus there is a disparity.
Now, one might object: since a convention (*saṅketa*) is observed in the case of words such as "Devadatta,"...
Why is it not assumed that even in the case of words such as "cow" (*go*), the convention (*saṅketa*) itself is what existed previously? No;
because [such an assumption] is subverted by a counter-inference (*pratyanumāna*).
For in that very case, one can formulate the following inference: "The men of former times [applied the word 'cow'] to an object possessing a dewlap and so forth..."

"Those who possess the comprehension of meaning from words such as 'cow' do so because they possess knowledge of the capacity [of words] established through the linguistic usage of elders, since they are capable of comprehending objects possessing dewlaps and so forth, just like people of the present day.
Thus, when that inference has been refuted by a counter-inference (pratyanumāna),
the non-human origin of the relationship between word and meaning is established precisely due to the absence of any means of valid cognition [to the contrary].
Therefore, this [argument] is refuted,
as the outsiders (Bāhyas) have said: "Whatever is established from whatever cause belongs to that same class, like fire and wood" (Pramāṇavārttika, Pariccheda 3, verse 243).
The demonstration of the beginninglessness of the usage of elders:
Now, this desire might indeed be fulfilled if the succession of the usage of elders were beginningless; however, that has been refuted by the ancient masters.
To this we reply:
Let it be granted that everything possessing parts has its existence originated through the conjunction of those parts, and that it is perishable upon the dissolution of the conjunction of its parts.
Nevertheless, there is no evidence for the claim that the entire [universe] arises and perishes at one and the same time;
on the contrary, it is more appropriate to conclude this based on what is observed: namely, that their emergence occurs sequentially.
And there is a gradual dissolution as well.

Furthermore, it can indeed be inferred that just as people of the present time obtain their selfhood based on the union of mother and father, so too did previous people, because they were likewise human beings.
Furthermore, it is not logical that the birth of those born without a womb occurs through the sovereign power of merit alone,
nor that of those born from moisture through the sovereign power of demerit alone— just as in the case of moisture-born beings—
because such [exclusive] observation is absent for those born from a womb or from an egg.
For inference everywhere follows what has been observed;

therefore, since [non-birth] is not invariably observed among those born of moisture (*saṃsvedaja*), it cannot be inferred that those born from a womb (*jarāyuja*) or from an egg (*aṇḍaja*) are also non-born from a womb (*ayonija*).
Indeed, one cannot infer fire from mere whiteness, even if it is steam.
However, just as a white substance is invariably determined to be fire, it is only such a thing that is fit to be its inferential mark;
[this concludes] the refutation of God.
Furthermore, as for this which was stated— that dharma and adharma are presided over by a preeminent state of volition—
that too is simply unproven;
for those two belong to that very *kṣetrajña* (knower of the field).
Let that very [self] be the controller.
If it is argued that its status as a controller is untenable because of its ignorance, then how could it be tenable for anyone else either?
For even for him, knowledge of dharma and adharma residing in another person is not possible, due to the absence of a cause;
indeed, his own sense organs are not the cause [of such knowledge].
Because the capacity of the sense faculties is not observed there;
nor is it the mind alone,
since the mind alone does not operate with respect to external objects.
For an Īśvara devoid of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) cannot have a connection with the sense organs and the mind, because that connection is dependent upon merit and demerit.
Alternatively, there must be some other cause for the cognition of the Īśvara.
That is incorrect,
because the cause of cognition is well-established;
for the causes of cognition are indeed well-known.
For it is logical that whatever effect is seen to have a certain cause must indeed possess that very cause;
otherwise, since an axe is seen to be presided over by a conscious agent, [it would follow that all things are so presided over].
How, then, can even merit and demerit be presided over by that [Lord]?
If it is argued that the intellect of the Lord is eternal and without cause,
that too is unsatisfactory.
Because the principle of intellect (buddhitattva) lacks permanence,
if it were permanent, it would not be intellect at all;
moreover, it is observed that [the body] is presided over by an intelligent being.
Nor by anything else.
Now, if the eternity of the Buddha is accepted even though it is unperceived,
then why is it not likewise accepted that he is devoid of the governance of consciousness?
Now, if it is argued that once the status of being a controller (*adhiṣṭhātṛtva*) is established, knowledge (*jñāna*) may also be postulated [as a concomitant],
[we reply: since there is no cause for a state of control that is not connected with knowledge and so forth, and since it is impossible to infer [such a state] when knowledge has been refuted.
Therefore, one must accept the pervasion (vyāpti) that only that which is capable of being known is insentient yet presided over by a sentient being,
because it is observed to be so;
for carpenters and others are seen to preside only over tools such as axes and the like, which are capable of being known, and not over others.
Furthermore, the purpose of the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) must also be considered.
It cannot be conjunction (saṃyoga), because since dharma and adharma are qualities (guṇa), they lack conjunction.
Furthermore, inherence (*samavāya*) is also untenable for God with respect to merit and demerit, which inhere in other persons;
for in the case of axes and such tools, the basis of the carpenter's action is simply the conjunction of his hands and so forth.
Likewise, what kind of activity could [inherence] possibly possess?
It cannot be action,
because action does not exist in dharma and adharma, which are themselves subordinate factors;
nor can it be origination, if [that is what you mean].

In that case, it [the fruit] arises from the *kṣetrajña* itself as the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), from the contact between the self and the mind as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), and being assisted by instrumental causes (*nimittakāraṇa*) such as intention (*abhisandhi*).
If you say, "It is the granting of the fruit," [we reply:]...
The fruit arises solely from merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) when accompanied by auxiliary conditions such as place, time, and state;
it does not depend upon the activity of a conscious agent.
This is the refutation of the God (*īśvara*) postulated by the Vaiśeṣikas.
As for what some say— that atoms themselves proceed by the power of the Lord's will— that too is not tenable, because such a form of superintendence is not observed in any instance.
If it is argued that such a thing is not observed in the body, we say no;
for that [body] is governed by the merit and demerit of the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field),
whereas the atoms themselves are not governed by the merit and demerit of Īśvara.
And its activity does not occur by mere will,
but rather through the power of effort;
nor is there even a cause for that will.
Nor is desire eternal,
for that would entail the consequence of constant activity; moreover, just as [the body] is inferred to be presided over by a conscious being because it is non-conscious, so too [is the case here].
Likewise, it is understood that there is no presiding [deity] due to the absence of purpose. We now consider which of these two forms of inference is more powerful:
[the inference from] "wherever there is a purpose," [or the other].
Therefore, the pervasion— that what is insentient is presided over by a sentient being— must be accepted,
because it is observed to be so.
Furthermore, inference is preceded by the apprehension of such a pervasion.
Pervasion is understood through both positive and negative concomitance;
and just as it is recognized that there must be an intelligent supervisor, so too is it recognized that he must possess a body and other such attributes.
Therefore, an inference proceeding in such a manner would only lead to the inference of something of that same nature.
Furthermore, since his status as a presiding agent over dharma and adharma, or over atoms, is not established, he is simply non-presiding.

Therefore, one must accept the following pervasion (*vyāpti*): that which is insentient and possesses the capacity to serve as a substratum for a body and so forth is necessarily presided over by a sentient being.

But if this were the case, would it not follow that even well-established inferences, such as that from smoke, would be abolished? For in those cases, the pervasion is understood through [smoke] existing in a kitchen or similar location, which is of such a nature [as you describe].
There is no inference regarding such a thing; rather,
there is no failure to ascertain at the time of the cognition of pervasion that which is of the same nature as that for which an inference is made.
That is incorrect— for the apprehension of a relation occurs in a general sense, by setting aside specific adjuncts such as place and time.
Therefore, in this case as well, whatever has been observed in the case of axes and the like applies equally to merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).
Only that form which is perceived as pervading can be inferred, and nothing else; and in this case, even the possession of a body and so forth enters into the pervasion.
If it is argued that it should be inferred from that [the body],
yet it cannot be so inferred,
then it is better to abandon the inference of consciousness, since that [consciousness] is not invariably concomitant with it.
Therefore, because there is an absence of a logical reason (hetu) for inferring the omniscience of God, there is a certainty of the absence of knowledge [in Him].
Consequently, only the beginningless tradition of usage by elders is the cause for understanding the meaning of words;
nor is there a convention established by God at the beginning of creation.
Because it is impossible for a convention to be created [all at once]:

indeed, people of the present day do not adopt a convention without first understanding the meaning of the sentence of that convention. Therefore, one must accept an beginningless succession of usage among the elders.

Thus, since there is no means for a person to comprehend *dharma* apart from the Word (*śabda*), it is not possible for the Veda to possess authority regarding its own subject matter—the unprecedented effect (*apūrvakārya*)—if it were of human origin. This concludes the demonstration of the non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the Vedas. How, then, is the non-human origin of the Vedas established?
It is said: [The Veda is not the work of an author] because no author is remembered.

Furthermore, an inference regarding an author is also not tenable; for when an object is not apprehended through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is impossible for words to be composed by those who lack direct perception of that object.
Even the designation "Kāṭhaka" and so forth is not sufficient to establish the actual existence of an author,
since that can be accounted for by the act of recitation alone;
furthermore, the mantras and arthavādas are not capable of conveying meaning independently.

However, according to the injunctions of the Vedic rules, their meaning conforms to those; thus, it is established that they possess authority in conveying established facts (*siddhārtha*), and that the relationship between word and meaning is non-human in origin (*apauruṣeya*).
This collyrium for the eyes, composed by Śālikanātha, is intended to dispel the darkness of false reasoning that obstructs the vision of his disciples.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Pure Ointment" (*vimalāñjana*), in the *Prakaraṇapañcikā* composed by the Great Professor, the venerable Śālikanātha Miśra.
